why: Two properties survive every alternative found, and both are the delivery half, not the storage half. (a) Identity is DERIVED, never declared: lane_for() resolves cwd by longest prefix (bus.py:85-110) and there is no register step to forget. Every alternative that has identities requires one -- MCP Agent Mail's README says outright "call ensure_project, then register_agent", JADE requires registration with the AMS, A2A requires a served Agent Card, and Redis/NATS require a client to name its own consumer group. bus.py's docstring names the failure this came from (23 personas sat undeployed because the step that required someone to remember never ran), so a registration handshake is not a small tax here, it is the defect. (b) Delivery is PUSHED at the operator's turn boundary because `python bus.py inbox` is registered on UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart in the live settings.json (dot-claude/settings.json:79-86, 173-180). An MCP tool cannot be pushed: Agent Mail's README delivers via `fetch_inbox`, which the model must decide to call, and "reading is a hook, not a habit" is this module's third design rule. Claude Code's own native Mailbox IS pushed and is the one real threat to (b), but its doc states "One team per session: a session has exactly one team, scoped to that session. You can't create additional named teams or share a team across sessions" and the team config directory is removed when the session ends -- which is precisely the job here, six independently launched terminals in four different directories that outlive each other. I am NOT claiming the storage half is unique: SQLite queues, git, Redis Streams and NATS all do durable ordered delivery with a per-consumer cursor better than 90 lines of JSONL append plus torn-line healing, and git already provides a stronger tamper-evident chain over the very same git-tracked file. That concession is the counterargument below, and it is the honest reason this record is not a rubber stamp: the verdict rests on roughly 250 lines of identity-and-delivery code, not on the other 600.

alternatives.name: Claude Code native agent-teams Mailbox (Anthropic, code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams, fetched 2026-07-29)
alternatives.covers: the closest match on mechanism and the only alternative that also PUSHES: the doc states each agent's mailbox is a JSON file at ~/.claude/teams/{team-name}/inboxes/{agent-name}.json, messages are "delivered automatically to recipients" with no polling, malformed entries are validated out while valid ones still deliver, and a shared task list with file-locked claiming comes with it. First-party, zero install, already on this machine.
alternatives.gap: checkable and quoted from the Limitations section: "One team per session: a session has exactly one team, scoped to that session. You can't create additional named teams or share a team across sessions", and the Architecture section says "The team config directory is removed when the session ends". Teammates are SPAWNED BY A LEAD, so six terminals the operator launched himself in four different repos are not a team and cannot address each other. Team names are session-derived (`session-` plus 8 chars of the session ID), so there is no stable lane address that outlives a session. It is also gated behind CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, "experimental and disabled by default". Nothing in the doc mentions integrity checking of a mailbox file beyond schema validation.
alternatives.cost: free and already installed; costs an env var. Token cost is the real cost: the doc warns agent teams "use significantly more tokens than a single session" because each teammate is a separate Claude instance, whereas bus.py moves text between terminals the operator was already running.
alternatives.maturity: first-party and actively developed; the fetched page cites behaviour changes at v2.1.178, .181, .186, .198, .199 and .207, so it is moving fast. I did NOT enable the flag or observe an inboxes/*.json file on this machine -- every claim here is quoted from the doc, not from a running system.

alternatives.name: MCP Agent Mail (github.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail, MIT, FastMCP + Git + SQLite; mcpagentmail.com)
alternatives.covers: the strongest real off-the-shelf competitor, and it covers more surface than bus.py: persistent memorable agent identities, inbox/outbox, threaded messages with acknowledgement, advisory file-reservation leases, FTS5 search over history, a Human Overseer channel, git-backed human-auditable artifacts, and it explicitly targets heterogeneous fleets (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI) coordinating on one codebase across independently launched sessions. Its git-backed store arguably beats bus.py's 16-hex chain on integrity, and Ed25519 signing exists on export bundles.
alternatives.gap: two hard misses against this component's own rules, both quotable from the README: identity is explicitly registered ("Register an identity: call ensure_project, then register_agent using this repo's absolute path as project_key"), not derived from cwd; and delivery is pull-based ("check inbox with fetch_inbox and acknowledge with acknowledge_message"), so the inbox arrives only when the model chooses to call a tool. Adopting it and preserving push delivery means writing a UserPromptSubmit hook that shells into its CLI anyway, on top of a server that must be up. Third miss: it needs a long-lived MCP server on port 8765, so the hook gains a network/liveness failure mode in a path that must never exit nonzero.
alternatives.cost: Python 3.14 via uv, FastMCP + uvicorn + SQLite + a git repo per project, a daemon on port 8765, 34 MCP tools' worth of tool-schema surface in every session's context. Replaces a zero-dependency stdlib script with a running service.
alternatives.maturity: repo and product site are both live as of 2026-07-29 and the project has a commercial companion stack, which suggests real investment. I did NOT install it, did NOT verify release cadence, star count, or issue activity, and did NOT verify it runs on Windows -- the README's installer touches .zshrc/.bashrc and says nothing about Windows, which for this machine is the single most important unverified fact in this record.

alternatives.name: A2A / Agent2Agent Protocol (Linux Foundation, v1.0 April 2026, 150+ organisations)
alternatives.covers: the industry standard for agent-to-agent messaging: Agent Cards for capability discovery, HTTP plus JSON-based message exchange, task delegation across vendors and networks. If this bus ever needs to talk to something that is not a Claude Code terminal on this laptop, this is the wire format to speak.
alternatives.gap: it standardises the wire, not the runtime. A Claude Code CLI session is not an HTTP-served agent with an Agent Card and has no listening endpoint, so adopting A2A means first building the very server that bus.py exists to avoid. The spec carries no durable inbox, no per-consumer cursor, no exactly-once replay for a crashed terminal, and no cwd-derived identity; a 2026 arXiv paper found in search ("Governance Gaps in Agent Interoperability Protocols: What MCP, A2A, and ACP Cannot Express") argues the governance layer is missing from all three, which matches what is missing here.
alternatives.cost: an HTTP server per lane plus an SDK, for four terminals sharing one filesystem. Disproportionate by a wide margin at this scale.
alternatives.maturity: genuinely mature and governed: Linux Foundation press releases confirm the project launched June 2025, hit v1.0 in April 2026, and passed 150 organisations with production enterprise use. I did NOT check whether any A2A SDK ships a local filesystem or stdio transport that would remove the server requirement -- that is the specific thing that would re-open this.

alternatives.name: Redis Streams consumer groups / NATS JetStream durable consumers
alternatives.covers: the professional answer to the exact cursor problem bus.py solves by hand: a server-side per-consumer position, acknowledgement, redelivery of unacked messages, and fan-out to multiple consumer groups. NATS JetStream additionally offers producer dedup via Nats-Msg-Id for effectively-exactly-once. Both would make the row-id cursor, the replay-on-vanished-cursor rule, and the torn-line healing unnecessary.
alternatives.gap: both need a running broker, which contradicts the module's stated "no lock, no db, no daemon" constraint and puts a liveness dependency inside cmd_inbox, a function whose docstring says it must never exit nonzero because a failing UserPromptSubmit hook blocks the operator's prompt. Redis Streams is at-least-once by default (duplicates after a consumer crash unless the consumer is idempotent). Neither derives a consumer identity from cwd, and neither leaves a git-diffable, human-readable log -- state/bus.jsonl is deliberately git-tracked and reviewed by eye.
alternatives.cost: a broker process plus a client library, on Windows, for four local terminals. Redis on Windows is not first-class.
alternatives.maturity: both long-established and actively documented in 2026 sources found in search. Not the failure point here; the failure point is that a daemon is the wrong shape for a hook.

alternatives.name: litequeue (litements/litequeue) and persist-queue (peter-wangxu/persist-queue)
alternatives.covers: durable local queues with no broker: SQLite-backed, ACID, explicit done()/ack, crash-surviving, single-file with no dependencies beyond the standard library in litequeue's case. This is the correct library answer for the append/parse/cursor plumbing, and adopting either would delete append_row's torn-line healing (bus.py:193-215) and read_all's JSONDecodeError skip (bus.py:183-189) outright.
alternatives.gap: they are point-to-point work queues, not an addressed multi-lane log. There is no `to: ALL` broadcast, no per-lane independent cursor over one shared ordered log (a popped message is gone for everyone), no identity, no integrity chain, and -- decisive here -- a SQLite file is opaque to git diff, while state/bus.jsonl is git-tracked on purpose so the operator and a future session can read and merge the traffic as text.
alternatives.cost: litequeue is a single-file pip dependency; persist-queue is heavier and defaults to pickle serialization. Either is cheap in install terms and expensive in the one thing that matters: it converts a reviewable text log into a binary blob.
alternatives.maturity: both are real published PyPI projects with public repos, confirmed via search. I did NOT verify last-release dates, maintenance status, or Windows CI for either.

alternatives.name: git itself, as the integrity layer (git log -p state/bus.jsonl / git diff)
alternatives.covers: this is the honest adopt candidate for one slice. state/bus.jsonl is ALREADY git-tracked, so git already maintains a Merkle-DAG over exactly this file that is stronger, far better tested, and far more widely reviewed than 50 lines of hand-rolled sha256 chaining. The motivating incident in the docstring (a third party edited a delivered row's body from "gate is RED" to "gate is GREEN") shows in `git diff` as a modified line rather than an appended one, which is unmistakable. Adopting it would retire canonical/row_hash/row_altered/cmd_verify (bus.py:117-172, 373-426) and roughly 100 lines of the integrity selftest.
alternatives.gap: one gap, and it is the whole argument: nothing runs `git diff` on every prompt, and git cannot mark an individual row inside the text delivered to the model. bus.py checks row_altered on the READ path and prints an ALTERED banner above the suspect body (bus.py:335-338, mirrored in cmd_log at bus.py:355), because "a check nobody invokes at the moment of use is a check that reports rather than protects". git also cannot cover the 12 rows in the live log that predate chaining any better than bus.py can, and neither covers truncation of the newest rows, which bus.py states in its own verify output (bus.py:408-409).
alternatives.cost: zero install; negative code. The cost is entirely the lost read-path mark.
alternatives.maturity: git is not the risk. This is the alternative most likely to overturn the verdict on re-read.

alternatives.name: FIPA-ACL / JADE, and the Crosby-Wallach tamper-evident-log line of work
alternatives.covers: the academic prior art for both halves. FIPA-ACL is the standardised agent communication language (speech-act performatives, which is what this module's KINDS tuple of fact/ask/answer/claim/warn/done is a small hand-rolled version of), and JADE is its reference platform with an AMS for registration, a DF yellow-pages, and an ACC message channel. Crosby and Wallach's tamper-evident data structures (USENIX Security 2009) plus Certificate-Transparency-style Merkle logs are the rigorous version of the hash chain in bus.py:117-172.
alternatives.gap: JADE is a JVM agent platform whose AMS registration step is exactly the declare-yourself pattern this module refuses on the record, and its performative ontology is far more machinery than six kinds of note between four terminals; search surfaced no evidence of it being used in 2026 LLM coding-agent tooling. The Crosby-Wallach work gives a Merkle tree for efficient membership and consistency proofs against an untrusted server, which is a threat model bus.py explicitly disclaims: its docstring already concedes this is "tamper EVIDENT, not tamper proof, and it authenticates nobody" because every lane runs as the same OS user, so the extra rigour buys nothing here.
alternatives.cost: JADE is a JVM runtime. The academic constructions are papers, not installable components for this job.
alternatives.maturity: FIPA-ACL and JADE are long-established standards; a 2026 ScienceDirect entry for PEAK-ACL (a FIPA-compliant Python package) appeared in search, showing the line is not dead. I read search-result summaries only; I did NOT read the Crosby-Wallach paper or the PEAK-ACL paper directly.

evidence: Read in full: tools/bus/bus.py:1-857 (all of it, including the 66-line WHY-THIS-EXISTS docstring at bus.py:1-66 and the ~390-line selftest at bus.py:429-816) and tools/bus/backfill_session_telemetry.py:1-154. Read as the worked example: docs/prior-art/tools-gate.json:1-72. Read for wiring: dot-claude/settings.json:79-86 and :173-180 (the two live `python bus.py inbox` hook registrations), tools/refute/checks/bus_wired.py:1-60 (the four-part wiring check that replaced a substring grep), tools/audit/mutations/bus.py:1-40 (mutation specs, including two mutations that SURVIVED on 2026-07-25 and were real test defects). Ran locally, read-only except for the throwaway temp dirs the selftest creates and removes: `python tools/bus/bus.py selftest` -> all checks passed; `python tools/bus/bus.py verify` -> exit 0, 19 rows, 7 chained, 12 predate chaining, chain intact. Two pages fetched in full: code.claude.com/docs/en/agents and code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams. Two fetched via summarising fetch: mcpagentmail.com and the mcp_agent_mail README on GitHub. NOT VERIFIED, stated plainly: I did not install or run MCP Agent Mail, did not confirm it runs on Windows (its installer references .zshrc/.bashrc and the README is silent on Windows), and did not check its release cadence or issue activity. recheck: Run all four; any ONE of them re-opens this verdict. (1) `python -c "import urllib.request;print('One team per session' in urllib.request.urlopen('https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams').read().decode())"` -- if that prints False, or the page no longer says the team config directory is removed when the session ends, then Claude Code's native pushed Mailbox may now span independently launched sessions and this component is redundant. (2) `gh release list --repo Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail --limit 5` and `gh api repos/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail --jq '.pushed_at,.open_issues_count'`, then grep its current README for 'register_agent', 'fetch_inbox' and 'Windows' -- if identity can now be derived from cwd without a register call, OR it ships a push/hook delivery path, OR Windows support is documented, re-open. (3) WebSearch "Claude Code hooks cross-session message delivery UserPromptSubmit inbox" for a first-party cross-session delivery hook event. (4) WebSearch "A2A protocol local transport stdio filesystem SDK" -- an official non-HTTP local transport would make the standard usable here without a server per lane.
what_ours_does: 1011 lines across two files, and they are not one component. bus.py (857 lines) is the bus. backfill_session_telemetry.py (154 lines, read in full) has nothing to do with messaging: it is a one-shot script that seeds 10 hand-graded observations into intent_control_plane.policy's Thompson-bandit telemetry log, which had never received a row; it is misfiled in this directory and should move to tools/bus's neighbour or to intent-control-plane. Everything below is bus.py. It is an append-only JSONL A2A bus for parallel Claude Code terminals, addressed by LANE. A lane is derived from cwd by longest-prefix match over a 4-entry map, lowercased for Windows path-case drift (bus.py:85-110); DEFAULT_LANE 'A' catches anything unmapped. A row carries id/ts/from_lane/origin_lane/from_session/to/kind/subject/body/refs/prev/hash, kind drawn from a fixed 6-tuple (bus.py:100). cmd_send (bus.py:266-292) chains each row to the previous row's id and hashes the result; --from-lane exists to break the derive-never-declare rule, so origin_lane records the cwd-derived lane BESIDE the declared one and the mismatch is printed to the reader at delivery time (bus.py:290, 325-328). Integrity: canonical() (bus.py:124-134) is a fixed wire format, sorted keys, no whitespace, absent keys OMITTED rather than defaulted so adding a CHAIN_FIELD later cannot silently rehash every historical row; row_hash is 16 hex of sha256; row_id (bus.py:142-156) returns the STORED hash for a chained row rather than a recomputation, specifically so tampering with the row a cursor names does not force a full replay; row_altered (bus.py:159-172) is checked on the READ path, not only by verify, and returns False for pre-chaining rows because those make no claim about their own content. Delivery: unread() (bus.py:246-263) walks BACKWARD from the end for the cursor's row id and, when the cursor names a row no longer in the file, REPLAYS from the start rather than skipping -- a deliberate choice of over-delivery over silent loss, because the defect it replaced was a positional cursor that silently ate a genuinely unread message after a hand-resolved git merge dropped an earlier line. An all-digits cursor is honoured once as the legacy positional form (bus.py:258-259). cmd_inbox (bus.py:295-346) wraps everything in a bare except that returns 0, because it is registered as a UserPromptSubmit hook and a failing hook blocks the operator's prompt; a tampered row is still DELIVERED but delivered marked with a three-line ALTERED banner (bus.py:335-338), and cmd_log carries the same mark (bus.py:355) so the two read surfaces cannot disagree. Durability plumbing: read_all skips a torn concurrent append instead of crashing (bus.py:183-189); append_row writes a newline first when the file does not end in one (bus.py:193-215), because otherwise one crashed write eats TWO messages, the fragment and its successor. cmd_verify (bus.py:373-426) exits 1 on any break, names unchained rows separately as uncovered rather than failing on them (--strict fails on them too), and prints its own blind spot: truncation of the newest rows is not detectable because nothing outside the file records the tip. cmd_selftest (bus.py:429-816) is roughly 30 assertions, each a property that broke in production or could break silently: the self-lane delivery regression that made 8 of the first 9 messages permanently undeliverable, exactly-once, peek-does-not-consume, torn line, corrupt cursor, longest-prefix lane derivation, tamper detection at read time AND the mark not firing on clean rows, mid-chain deletion sent through cmd_send rather than the test's own writer (a mutation showed planting tested the test), a pinned golden canonical byte string and digest at bus.py:668-689 as a fixed external oracle for the wire format, and the legacy positional cursor. Live state at review time: state/bus.jsonl, 19 rows, 7 chained, 12 pre-chaining, verify exit 0.
strongest_counterargument: About 600 of the 857 lines are storage and integrity plumbing that better-tested software already does, and the record defends them by pointing at the 250 lines that are genuinely unique. Take the integrity half first: state/bus.jsonl is git-tracked. Git already maintains a Merkle-DAG over that exact file, and the motivating incident -- a third party editing a delivered row's body from RED to GREEN -- appears in `git diff` as a modified line, distinguishable at a glance from an appended one. canonical, row_hash, row_altered, cmd_verify and roughly 100 lines of selftest (bus.py:117-172, 373-426, plus the integrity cases) reimplement in 50 lines of hand-rolled sha256 a property git provides more strongly, and the module's own docstring already concedes the chain "authenticates nobody" and cannot detect truncation. Its only real advantage over git is the read-path ALTERED banner, and that is a formatting decision, not an integrity mechanism: the same banner could be driven from a `git diff --numstat` check. Now the storage half: append_row's torn-line healing and read_all's JSONDecodeError skip (bus.py:183-215) exist only because the transport is hand-rolled JSONL. stdlib sqlite3 -- zero new dependency, already in the interpreter, WAL mode, real atomic concurrent appends -- deletes both, and litequeue shows the shape. The honest verdict for this component is therefore arguably SPLIT, not keep-ours: keep lane_for, the row-id cursor, the never-exit-nonzero hook entry point and the replay-not-skip rule (roughly 250 lines with no off-the-shelf equivalent under these constraints), and retire the hash chain to git and the JSONL append path to sqlite3. The two counters to that are real but neither is free: the git-tracked plain-text log is deliberately human-diffable and merge-resolvable, which sqlite3 destroys; and nothing runs git diff on every prompt. And the broader threat is bigger than either: Anthropic shipped a pushed, file-backed, validated Mailbox into Claude Code itself. Its only disqualifying limitation today is one sentence in a doc marked experimental -- "You can't create additional named teams or share a team across sessions". If that sentence changes, this entire component becomes a worse copy of a first-party feature, and the record should be re-opened on that sentence alone rather than waiting for the October date.
